conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for taking a few minutes to talk with me. I’m Dr. Morales, a perinatal mental-health clinician who works with new mothers. I’ll be guiding you through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s a brief, well-studied questionnaire that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived—especially over the past seven days. Nothing you share leaves this room, and there are no “right” or “wrong” answers; we simply want to hear your honest experience so we can make sure you’re getting the support you deserve.

We’ll go through 10 questions together. I’ll ask each one conversationally, and you can answer in your own words. If any question feels difficult, we can pause or skip it—just let me know.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:

Over the past week, have you still been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt harder to do lately?

Honestly, laughing feels kind of forced lately. My husband will make a joke or something silly will happen with the baby, and I’ll smile, but it’s like the joy doesn’t quite reach me the way it used to. I *want* to laugh, but mostly I just feel this heaviness sitting on my chest.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I wish that were true for me. I can smile, and sometimes I’ll let out a little laugh, but it feels thin—like I’m doing it because I know I’m supposed to, not because anything actually feels funny inside.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels like one more thing I have to get through. Some days I’ll think, “Maybe tomorrow I’ll feel like myself again,” but when tomorrow comes, the spark just isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that almost every day. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m not soothing him right, or if I can’t get him to nap I assume I’m doing something wrong as a mom. Last night he spit up a lot after feeding and I just sat there crying, convinced it was my fault for eating something “bad.” Rationally I know babies just spit up, but the guilt still jumps on me.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much all the time. Even when the baby’s sleeping peacefully, I’ll suddenly worry his breathing sounds different, or I’ll imagine him choking and have to check the monitor every few minutes. There’s no real reason—everything can be quiet, and my heart’s still racing like something awful is about to happen.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… a few times this week I’ve been hit with this sudden wave of panic—like I’m standing on the edge of something terrible, even if nothing’s actually happening. Once, I was just folding laundry in the nursery and my chest got tight, heart pounding, couldn’t catch my breath. It passed after a minute, but it left me shaky and on edge the rest of the afternoon.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. It feels like the minute I finish one thing—feeding, changing, pumping—there’s already another mess or cry waiting. I keep a little mental checklist and it just keeps growing. Some mornings I wake up already exhausted by everything I “should” do, and by bedtime I’m running on fumes. I haven’t broken down completely, but I’m constantly on the edge of tears.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

That’s been happening several nights. I’ll lie down exhausted, but my mind keeps circling—did I sterilize the bottles right, is the baby breathing, am I already failing him—so I can’t drift off. Even when I do sleep, I wake up with my heart racing and can’t settle back for a while. I’d guess I’m actually getting maybe four broken hours a night.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah, that’s most days now. It’s like a gray cloud follows me around. I’ll look at the baby and feel like I should be glowing, but instead I feel empty or just… flat. I’ll cry in the shower so nobody sees, then wipe my face and keep going. It’s not every single second, but it’s definitely the background music of my days.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes… a couple of times this week it just spilled over. Yesterday I sat in the glider after finally getting him down, and instead of feeling relieved I felt this wave of sadness and started sobbing. I tried to stay quiet so I wouldn’t wake him. It’s like the tears come whether I want them to or not.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

…once or twice, fleeting. I’ll be rocking the baby in the middle of the night and suddenly picture myself stepping into a hot shower and just—well, never coming back out. It’s never a plan, more like a scary postcard that flashes in my head and then disappears. It shakes me up, because I don’t want to leave him—I just want the heaviness to stop.

You've shared that the joy of new motherhood feels distant right now-laughter is thin, activities you once loved seem like chores, and a constant gray cloud of sadness, worry, and self-blame follows you. Nights are restless, tears come without warning, and frightening thoughts of escaping the heaviness sometimes flash through your mind, though you desperately want to stay and care for your baby.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished enjoyment and forced laughter, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily self-blame, attributing normal infant behaviors to personal maternal failure.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive, intrusive worries occurring 'pretty much all the time' with physical anxiety symptoms and no rational trigger, matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden intense panic episodes with physical symptoms (tight chest, pounding heart, breathlessness) occurring multiple times this week, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent overwhelm and feeling unable to keep up with daily tasks, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to racing anxious thoughts, averaging only four broken hours—clearly "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness ('most days now,' 'background music of my days'), emptiness, frequent crying, and emotional flatness—clearly matching 'Yes, most of the time.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes this week with uncontrollable sobbing, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 25 places you well above the 14-point threshold for probable major depression; item scores show loss of interest/pleasure, daily low mood, prominent anxiety and panic, disrupted sleep, and self-blame. These patterns align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>, supported by your reports of <quote>gray cloud</quote> and <quote>background music of sadness</quote>. Item 10 score ≥1 mandates urgent safety review. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal psychiatrist within 24-48 hours
2. Complete formal face-to-face suicide-risk assessment and develop 24-hour safety/support plan
3. Begin evidence-based psychotherapy (CBT or interpersonal therapy) specializing in postpartum mood
4. Discuss benefits/risks of antidepressant compatible with breastfeeding if indicated
5. Arrange practical help-partner/family to cover night feeds when possible and share household tasks
6. Encourage 20-30 minutes of daylight and gentle movement daily; reduce self-expectations
7. Provide 24-hour crisis hotline numbers and local emergency contacts
8. Re-screen EPDS in 2 weeks to track response to interventions
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Screening Note – Postpartum Visit  
Date: [today]  
Source: self-report on 10-item EPDS-style questionnaire  

1. Primary endorsed symptoms  
   – Persistent low mood, anhedonia, excessive self-blame/guilt  
   – Marked anxiety (generalized & panic-type episodes)  
   – Sleep disruption secondary to rumination  
   – Daily tearfulness, feeling “on the edge of tears”  
   – Sense of being overwhelmed by routine infant care  

2. Observed patterns  
   – Symptoms present “most days” x ≥2 wks  
   – Pleasure/interest markedly reduced for previously enjoyed activities  
   – Cognitions dominated by “not doing motherhood right”  
   – Physiologic arousal (racing heart, breathlessness) without clear trigger  

3. Screening significance  
   – Meets clinical threshold concern for Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety features  
   – Functional impact: impaired sleep, caregiving stress, social withdrawal  

4. Safety  
   – Endorses passive suicidal ideation (no plan, no intent); transient mental image of “never coming back out” of shower.  
   – Protective factor: strong desire to remain with infant.  
   → Requires immediate safety assessment and development of 24-hr support plan.  

5. Next screening steps (document for provider)  
   – Administer formal EPDS score; consider PHQ-9/GAD-7  
   – Evaluate suicide risk in face-to-face interview  
   – Review supports, sleep hygiene, infant care demands  
   – Consider referral to perinatal psychiatry/therapy; discuss medication compatibility if breastfeeding  

Clinician signature / date
